## Overview

The Standard Normal distribution is our baseline case. Since the population is already normal, the CLT should work immediately — even at very small sample sizes. This gives us a reference point to compare all other distributions against.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(1278)
B <- 10000
library(moments)
```

## 1. What Does the Population Look Like?

```{r}
#| label: population-plot

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Standard Normal Population",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
```

The Standard Normal distribution is perfectly symmetric and bell-shaped with mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1.

**Theoretical mean:** 0\
**Theoretical standard deviation:** 1

## 2. My Prediction

Since the population is already normal, I expect the sampling distribution of the mean to look normal at every sample size, even n = 1. This distribution should converge the fastest of all the ones we test.

## 3. Monte Carlo Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulation

n_values <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100)

results <- data.frame(
  n              = n_values,
  simulated_mean = NA,
  simulated_sd   = NA,
  theoretical_se = NA,
  se_difference  = NA,
  skewness       = NA,
  kurtosis       = NA
)

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
  
  sim_sd <- sd(sample_means)
  theo_se <- 1 / sqrt(n)
  
  results$simulated_mean[i]  <- mean(sample_means)
  results$simulated_sd[i]    <- sim_sd
  results$theoretical_se[i]  <- theo_se
  results$se_difference[i]   <- round(abs(sim_sd - theo_se), 5)
  results$skewness[i]        <- skewness(sample_means)
  results$kurtosis[i]        <- kurtosis(sample_means)
}
```

## 4. Results Table

```{r}
#| label: results-table

round(results, 4)
```

## 5. Simulated vs Theoretical Standard Error

For the Standard Normal distribution with σ = 1, the theoretical SE = 1/√n. Looking at the results table the simulated standard deviation of the sample means matches the theoretical standard error almost exactly at every sample size. The `se_difference` column confirms this — the differences are extremely small, essentially rounding error.

This is the ideal case. Because the population is already normal, both the shape and the spread of the sampling distribution behave exactly as theory predicts from the very start. This serves as our benchmark — every other distribution should eventually converge to this level of agreement between simulated and theoretical SE.

## 6. Histograms Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: histograms
#| fig-height: 10

par(mfrow = c(4, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
  
  hist(sample_means, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE,
       main = paste("n =", n),
       xlab = "Sample Mean", col = "steelblue", border = "white")
  
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(n)),
        add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 7. Q-Q Plots Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
#| fig-height: 10

par(mfrow = c(4, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
  
  qqnorm(sample_means, main = paste("Q-Q Plot: n =", n),
         col = "steelblue", pch = 20, cex = 0.3)
  qqline(sample_means, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 8. Conclusion

The sampling distribution of the Standard Normal mean is approximately normal at every sample size tested, including n = 1. This is expected since we are sampling from a normal population — the mean of normal random variables is itself normal regardless of sample size.

**My "normal enough" standard:**

- Histogram is visually bell-shaped and symmetric
- Q-Q plot points fall close to the reference line with no systematic curves
- Skewness is between -0.5 and 0.5
- Kurtosis is close to 3

**Answer for Standard Normal:** $$\boxed{n = 1}$$

The CLT is not needed here — the population is already normal, so the sampling distribution is normal at any sample size. The simulated SE matches the theoretical SE perfectly at every n, further confirming this.

## 9. What Surprised Me

Even at n = 1 the sampling distribution is perfectly normal and the simulated SE matches theory exactly. This makes sense mathematically but seeing it confirmed visually reinforces why the Standard Normal serves as the ideal baseline — it shows us what perfect normality looks like so we can compare it against the skewed and heavy-tailed distributions later.
